#8844. Try This Variation of Sun Salutation if You Have a Tight Back or Hamstrings

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about a Sun Salutation variation for tight hamstrings poses appeared in the September-October 1990 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Sun Salutations are a means of aligning your breath and movement in a cyclical, graceful way. The series of poses unfolds in a way you can get lost in, creating the type of flow state you’re often after on your mat.

This Sun Salutation variation provides some opportunities for altering poses for anyone who experiences tightness in the back or hamstrings while retaining the strengthening along with the calming breath and movement of a classic Sun Salutation (Surya Namaskar). More specifically, it skips Plank but includes poses such as Chaturanga and the ferocious Upward-Facing Dog (Urdhva Mukha Svanasana), inviting you to further work your arms, legs, and abdominals.

Looking for even more of a challenge? Try hopping or jumping between poses when it makes sense for you.

Begin with your hands by your sides or at heart center in Mountain Pose.

Stretch your arms over the head and look slightly toward the sky in Upward Salute. If you want, bring your palms together and press.

Keep your knees bent as you bend forward with your arms extended over the head. Feel as if you are lifting your soft frontal body (the abdomen, organs, and lungs) into the shell of your back body (the pelvis, spine, and rib cage) so your spinal muscles do not overwork.

As you hang in Standing Forward Bend, begin to lift your sit bones upward, so the legs begin to straighten a little and your pelvis tips farther forward over your feet. You will feel an increased stretch along the back of the legs as the knees straighten. If you feel strain in the back of the knees or the lower back, keep your knees bent.

On an inhalation, step your left leg back behind you in Low Lunge. Allow your left knee to bend slightly or lower to the floor and make sure that your right knee is directly over your right ankle. If this pose puts too much strain on your lower back or groin, rest your hands on two blocks placed on either side of your forward foot.

Exhale to place your hands on the your mat and step back to Downward-Facing Dog. In this version, bring the feet hip-width apart, lifting the sitting bones and keeping the knees bent if needed. Keep the sitting bones lifted as you lower the heels toward the floor.

The most common mistake in the practice of Chaturanga is to bring the shoulders all the way forward over the wrists without bending the elbows. Lowering the chest from this position requires tremendous arm strength and almost invariably results in lowering the belly first and then collapsing the chest onto the floor. Lowering the knees to the floor can help.

On an exhalation, gently lower the knees to the floor and shift the chest forward until it is directly over the hands. Keep the elbows close to the rib cage as they bend, lowering the torso toward the ground without bending through the middle of the spine. If your arm strength is insufficient to prevent the middle of the spine from collapsing, you may want to do Plank Pose instead.

keep the abdomen lifted into the lower back as the chest lowers to just above the floor. Press back through your heels to elongate the spine.

Keeping the knees lightly on the floor, inhale and press the hands into the floor to straighten the arms. As the arms straighten, come onto the tops of the feet and broaden the shoulders, rolling the base of the shoulder blades down and forward in Upward-Facing Dog. Draw the belly back into the body, to support the lumbar spine, and lengthen the abdomen upward toward the chest. This variation creates a less extreme curve in the lumbar spine than the straight-legged version. You can always lower your chest closer to the floor if the backbend feels too extreme.

Move through Downward-Facing Dog, Standing Forward Bend, and Upward Salute, finishing with your hands together at heart center in Mountain Pose.

#8842. Turn Your Pool Workout Into Playtime With These Game-Inspired Exercises

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Turn your swim workouts into games with these fun ideas for making the pool more enjoyable. (Photo: Challenge Family)

We know all the excuses to skip a swim because we’ve used many of them ourselves. Either it’s too cold outside or it’s too beautiful a day to pass up a bike ride. Or perhaps there’s a storm 100 miles away that might suddenly decide to blow right over the aquatics center. But the truth is, if your workout is interesting enough, you’ll have all the excuses you need to get yourself into the pool, not out of it.

And we’re not just talking about adding in a random drill here and there. Gamifying your swim workout, whether through solo exercises or team activities, helps make a workout enticing enough that you’ll want to do it over and over again. Adding an element of play to your swim can make it more challenging, productive, and fun all at once.

Before we get into a handful of our favorite games and drills, we asked Sage Hopkins, head coach of Women’s Swimming & Diving at San José State University, for his tips on how to make swimming more enjoyable. With these tools in your arsenal, you might not skip your pool workouts anymore, but actually look forward to them instead.

First, Hopkins stresses how crucial it is to hear laughter echoing across the pool deck. This might not be possible if you’re training alone, but if you have a training buddy who always keeps you smiling, make it a priority to meet with them more regularly. Hopkins also encourages using music to establish an upbeat atmosphere; that might look like playing a pump-up song on your way to the pool, or investing in a pair of swimming headphones to keep the tunes going lap after lap.

Once you know your purpose, Hopkins says, it’s easier to figure out what kinds of activities will make swimming more meaningful and enjoyable. Those who enjoy the camaraderie aspect of swimming and triathlon will enjoy team games like sharks and minnows.

Even simple details like naming a set, Hopkins says, can add a thrill to swimming. If there’s a test set you’re always dreading, give it a quirky or amusing name to make it seem less intimidating. You could use the most challenging triathlon you’ve ever lined up for as inspiration (The Wales One Hundreds, for instance, or the Norseman No Breathers).

Now, without further ado, let the games begin!

You don’t need any fancy clubs to play a round of swim golf — just enough glycogen in your head to add numbers. Hopkins suggests this drill for data-driven triathletes because it’s easy to keep track of your progression over time. Essentially, you add the number of strokes with the number of seconds that it takes you to complete a certain distance (such as 50 yards) to get a “score.” You’ll then repeat that distance several times within a single set, trying to keep your score as low as possible. This game helps improve your distance per stroke and ultimately conserve energy.

Healthy suspense invites bursts of dopamine and curiosity into your workout, and it also means that there’s no one to blame but fate for back-to-back sprint sets. Make sure to write the following rules down on a whiteboard or protected piece of paper to reduce confusion.

Start by grabbing a set of waterproof playing cards, and assign a technique to each suit; for example, spades might call for kicking, hearts for drills, diamonds for swimming, and clubs for pulling. Next, assign a distance to groups of numbers (for instance, 2s and 3s might mean 50s, while 4s and 5s might mean 100s, and so on). Keep your jacks, queens, kings, and aces in a separate pile because they’ll dictate the number of repeats (1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively).

So, for example, pulling a 5 of clubs alongside a queen would require you to grab your pull buoy for 2×100. Pulling a 2 of hearts alongside an ace would mean a 5×50 drill.

Another way to bring a measure of unpredictability to your workout is to roll a single die four times to determine your next set. The first roll determines your technique (5s could require kicking), the second your effort level (perhaps 4s always mean sprints), the third your distance (1s could mean 50s), and the fourth your number of reps (anywhere from 1 to 6).

If you were on a summer swim team as a kid, chances are high you played many games of sharks and minnows. The game starts out with one “shark” who tries to tag all the other “minnows” as they swim from one side of the pool to the other. Each swimmer who gets tagged turns into a shark for the next round. You can complicate this game by instituting an underwater safety zone.

If you have an area of the pool to yourself, form teams, set up goals on opposite walls with pull buoys, grab a ball, and play water polo. This is an excellent way to make vertical kicking, sprinting, and treading water more exciting. It also facilitates team bonding.

Head to the deep end for this game to work on endurance as you tread water and practice vertical kicking. If the lifeguards allow it, you can play water volleyball over the flags with an inflatable beach ball. Your pool might even have a water volleyball net, and some versions float so that you can move them as required.

Hopkins recommends “call it sets,” inspired by Bob Steele, to work on pacing and fine-tuning your internal clock. Essentially, you and your training partners will swim a set of 100s, and before each repeat, each one of you will predict the time you expect to hit. Whoever is closest to their estimates wins the set.

Chase sets are a fun way for training groups with seemingly disparate ability levels to unite, says Hopkins. Slower swimmers are allowed a head start, while faster swimmers are tasked with trying to catch them. Chase sets are ideally employed for speedwork, not drills.

Casino night is extraordinarily fun for large teams and helps highlight everyone’s unique talents. First, two or three swimmers who are roughly equivalent in speed line up at the blocks. Then, the other teammates line up behind the swimmer they predict will win.

From there, you’ll use cards or dice to determine the “event” that the swimmers will be competing in (see general rules above in the solo workouts). Whoever has picked the winning swimmer gets a rest break while the rest of the team completes a penalty swim (a 50 sprint, perhaps). If you have one seemingly unbeatable swimmer on the team, you can assign them a permanent handicap.

#8841. How Reverse-Grip Lat Pulldowns Helped Jay Cutler Build an Even Wider Back

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Mass monster Jay Cutler, who claimed the title of Mr. Olympia on four occasions between 2006 and 2010, was never afraid to step away from the barbell if there was an efficient way to sculpt his back. Recently, the bodybuilder revealed that he liked to begin each back session with cable reverse-grip pulldowns. Here’s why.

“This was always the first exercise I started my back routine with,” confirmed Cutler in a recent video for his 5.7 million IG followers.

Techniques used by Jay Cutler to string together 25 consecutive top 2 finishes.

Utilizing a supinated (underhand) grip, you’ll primarily tax the lats while also recruiting the biceps and mid back. For many, the supinated grip is more comfortable on the shoulders than the pronated (overhand) grip. So, seated at the cable station, you’ll replicate a similar movement with the upper body to a chin up as you lower the bar. This grip also allows for heavier loads, making it perfect for adding upper body mass.

Tip: Keep your torso still and pull with the elbows until the bar is lowered just under your chin. Don’t pull any further down, or the load will shift to your forearms and shoulders.

“When you do something, reverse grip, it’s going to give you more flexion in those lats. It’s going to allow you to pull a little deeper and engage certain fibers,” explained Cutler who, as a competitive bodybuilder, was all about lifting heavy weights to create a winning physique.

In his video, Cutler kept the distance between his hands a little over shoulder width. “Pull down, focus on 12 repetitions,” he added. The Olympia icon also explained that the reverse grip lat pulldown was essential to building the winged appearance of his lats. “So, when I was doing that front double bicep (pose), it really yanked those lats out,” shared the legend. “And created that great V-taper.”

For Jay Cutler, the reverse grip lat pulldown was key to building muscle thickness. To try it for yourself, avoid using momentum and concentrate on the muscle contraction instead, as you lower the bar. Then slowly allow the bar to return skywards for additional time under tension.

#8840. Clipless Pedals Can Feel Intimidating—Here Are Some Tips to Make Those First Clipless Rides Feel Smoother

Expert tips for cleat setup, pedal tension, and safe unclipping before your first ride.

When a rider switches from flat pedals to clipless pedals, they typically aren’t thinking about the differences of pedals like Shimano SPD or SPD-SL, Wahoo Speedplays, or egg-beater pedals. Many times, they haven’t heard of Time pedals or the different Assioma or Garmin models. The first thought many have is, “How do I get out of the pedal once I’m clipped in?”

Not all people considering the switch realize this—as contradictory as it sounds, clipless pedals refer to a pedal system where you are clipped into the pedal. If you aren’t familiar with the system, think about being clipped into a ski binding. Some pedal options offer different release settings—similar to how a DIN setting on a ski binding can be adjusted to offer different levels of force needed to release the ski boot from the binding.

Here we’ll dig into what clipless pedals are, how they can benefit you on your ride, tips for setting up your pedals and cleats, and tips for those daunting first few rides with your new pedals.

I have plenty of friends who swear by the saying, “flat pedals win medals.” However, there is a reason you’ll only see clipless pedals at world tour road races or on the majority of gravel bikes at your local gravel grinder. When you ride clipped in you end up using more of your leg musculature during each revolution of your pedal stroke.

In short, this means you’re typically more efficient when using clipless pedals compared to flat pedals. For clarity, you don’t need to ride clipless pedals to be a cyclist. But for those riders looking to take their riding to the next level, it’s worth giving them a try.

Because you’re literally attached to the pedal, you use not only your quads in the downstroke part of the revolution, but you also work your hamstrings, hip flexors, and glutes as you pull up. All of those muscles at work translate to more power while you’re riding, especially as you refine your pedaling technique. To get started, here’s your expert-backed guide to pedaling with clipless pedals—without falling over.

“Cleat placement is paramount,” says Issac Denham, owner of bike fitting studio Befitting Bicycles in Wayne, Pennsylvania. “Since incorrect cleat placement can lead to injuries, we suggest booking time with a bike fitter to place your cleats. Having a professional install your cleats also ensures that they won’t be installed improperly or even upside down.”

For those riders that want to try clipless pedals, but don’t want to jump into a precision fit, start with cleats in a neutral position. This means setting the cleats up in the middle of the slots in the shoe with the cleats relatively straight. Just make sure the left and right cleats are in roughly the same position—this will give you a good baseline moving forward.

It will take time doing the guess and check method for cleat placement, but this method gives you the chance to play around going clipless before you invest hundreds into a bike fit. If you start to develop pain after using clipless pedals, stop pedaling. This is likely due to cleat position and that is when it is time to see a local trusted shop for direction.

“Many clipless pedals have adjustable pedal tension. This is basically how hard the built-in spring holds the cleat in the pedal,” says Dan Chabonov, Bicycling test editor. “Setting this tension as low as possible means you need less force to clip in and out of the pedals and can make the learning process a little easier.”

While most clipless pedals already come set at the lowest tension setting from the manufacturer, you can also easily make the adjustment.

“Typically out of the box, pedals are set up with the least amount of release tension,” says Becky Quinn, former pro and bike fitter. “The pedal tensioner is on the rear of the pedal. There is a small 3mm bolt that requires a 3mm Allen wrench to adjust the tension. It can be turned counterclockwise to loosen the tension or clockwise to tighten it. There is a small window on the back of the pedal that has a small horizontal pin that moves up or down depending on which way you turn the tensioner.”

If you adjust the tension on your pedals, make sure you confirm that the pins are in the same place on both the left and right pedal, so the release tension is the same on both sides.

Practice does indeed make perfect when it comes to learning how to pedal with clipless pedals. The goal is to become so comfortable with the movements that they become part of your muscle memory, so you don’t have to look down at your foot or pedal for longer than a quick glance.

When you’re just starting out pedaling with clipless pedals, do it inside first. “Practicing indoors either on a trainer, or even leaned up against a wall, can be a great place to start where you don’t have to worry about falling down or looking silly,” says Denham.

When I ran a shop and was getting people set up on clipless pedals, I would suggest they get on the bike inside, ideally on a trainer or next to a wall to stabilize themselves, then put on a show or a movie. It sounds monotonous (and the people you live with might give you an odd look or two), but simply clip in, clip out, clip in, clip out, over and over. Do it looking down at your shoe, then when that’s comfortable practice doing it without looking down. Feel it out inside and you’ll be much better off when you head out the door.

To clip into your pedal, start with the pedal positioned at the bottom of the pedal stroke.

“Softly lift the front of the pedal with your toe to flip it over so that you can engage. Your toe will be slightly pointed downward. Slide your foot forward until the tongue of the cleat stops on the lip of the pedal,” Quinn explains. “Once you can’t slide your foot any further forward, continue to pedal forward and add pressure to the pedal. It will click in. Sometimes you will need to rotate your heel inward or outward at the 6 o’clock position to engage securely.”

Then it’s time to clip out: “In order to practice clipping out of your pedals, place one leg all the way down to the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock). Then, firmly rotate your heel outward. Be sure to not roll your ankle,” Quinn advises. “The motion should be similar to that of smashing a bug under the ball of your foot.”

If there is a single gem of advice we would love to pass on to every cyclist who has ever learned how to ride with clipless pedals, this would be it: Unclip the foot you intend to put down when you come to a stop before you come to a stop. “This is the most important piece of the puzzle,” says Quinn.

Once you unclip, “here is the most critical piece: Keep the unclipped foot on the pedal but continue to pedal a half stroke,” Quinn adds. “Once the foot that is still clipped in gets to the 6 o’clock position, coast and stand up. Your butt needs to get off the saddle. Continue to apply your rear brakes until you are almost at a stop. When you are about to come to a complete stop, apply your front brake and step down with the unclipped foot.”

Many cleat and pedal systems will follow a similar process with the general idea being: line up the cleat on the pedal and add downward force to clip in once the cleat is aligned.

Remember how we said switching to clipless pedals is a cycling rite of passage of sorts? Well, so is falling over as you’re learning. Practicing while riding on grass can make the falls a little easier, and falling with the proper technique (yes, there’s a technique for falling, too!) will lower your chances of serious injury.

“You will fall. We all have done it and it’s okay,” says Quinn. “Just remember that if you start to fall over, turn your buttocks so you land on it. It is the most padding we have on our bodies. Putting out an arm can break a wrist. You most likely will only get a bruise on your butt.”

The most important thing is not to get in your head, beat yourself up, or give up. Falling over at least a few times has happened to every single cyclist who rides with clipless pedals.

I’ll never forget one of my first rides with clipless pedals. I rolled over to the group in the parking lot overly confident, forgot I had to unclip my foot from the pedal, and slowly tipped over—still attached to the bike. It happens to everyone when you’re first making the switch, but some practice at home can make the transition a little less painful.

Natascha Grief is the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health. She writes about fitness, health, performance, everyday movement, and the products that help people train and recover better. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She previously worked as the health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and her writing has appeared in Runner’s World and other outlets. Across her work, she’s especially focused on making complex wellness, training, and performance topics approachable and accessible.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

Nick Walker is expected to hit the Arnold Classic stage in March, and if this heavy upper-body workout is anything to go by, “The Mutant” could be unstoppable in Columbus, OH, next year.

With the Arnold Classic now on his mind, the 2026 Mr. Olympia winner is hoping to top last year’s second place and rule this stage like he did last September at the Olympia. And, to get there, it appears that The Mutant is willing to push past his own superhuman limits. This was evidenced by a recent Instagram reel, in which Walker recorded a brutal but brilliant upper body session for his 2-million-plus followers.

With Olympia runner-up Samson Dauda speculated to enter, and Andrew Jacked confirming that he will try to defend his 2026 Arnold Classic trophy, Walker understands that each and every rep counts.

The 2026 Mr. Olympia found the ultimate success this time around with his outer sweep.

Walker’s video shows some seriously heavy sets, with the aim of reaching failure, so you should conduct some feeler sets to find the correct weight for you. For added safety, The Mutant is also spotted by IFBB Pro, Andy Paredes. “I’m not big on partners, but homie trains hard,” quipped Mr. Olympia in his IG caption.

The session started with the seated incline dumbbell press, a move that builds the shoulders, upper chest, and triceps. “Best chest on stage,” encouraged Paredes as Walker got ready to leave it all on the gym floor. “No weaknesses this year.”

Next up was the seated chest press machine, hitting the entire chest, shoulders, and triceps. Using the machine means that Walker can target these muscle groups effectively, while a traditional bench press requires the recruitment of the core for stabilization.

For his third exercise, The Mutant upped the anti with his chest dips, adding a plate suspended from his waist by a chain. And, if you are wondering what separates a chest dip from a triceps dip, it’s all about the positioning. Notice that Walker’s head and chest are forward, whereas triceps dips are characterized by a straighter torso. This way, the big man is activating the chest and anterior deltoids at the front of his shoulders

Moving on to the standing lateral raise machine, The Mutant turns his attention to the lateral (side) and rear deltoids, providing his upper body with a broader topline. Notice how he raises and then lowers the handles in a slow and controlled motion for added time under tension.

For his final exercise, Walker continues to build winning arms with standing barbell bicep curls, blasting those biceps and engaging the core to remain stable. Despite the heavy load, the 2026 Mr. Olympia once again concentrates on quality muscle contractions and time under tension.

To replicate these reps for yourself, aim for 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps on each exercise. The added weight on the chest dips is optional, but be sure to go heavy, taking in at least one feeler set to avoid injury. This may be a brutal workout, but the muscle building benefits could be brilliant.

#8836. What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March

Top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season. (Photo: FinisherPix/Triathlete, Aaron Palaian, Oliver Baker, and courtesy David Tilbury-Davis)

One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.

With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.

For Northern Hemisphere athletes, that time is now. So, to help you along the way, we turned to four of the sport’s leading coaches to get their views — in their words — on what triathletes should focus on between now and March.

One of the world’s leading coaches and applied sports scientists in endurance sport, Plews has coached elite triathletes, including world champions Chelsea Sodaro, Javier Gomez, and Terenzo Bozzone.

He is also the founder of the coaching platform Endure IQ for both athletes and coaches. Plews himself is a former age-group Ironman world champion and still holds the fastest amateur time at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship.

“I never did proper strength training when I was younger, but now that I do a lot more, I’m seeing the benefits. But it is only as good as the quality and intent you put in. One of the big mistakes I see with many triathletes is that there’s no real intent.

“Get someone to help make sure you’re doing proper lifts. If you need to learn the correct movements, winter would be an ideal time. Then strength work needs to challenge the system. We typically talk “reps in reserve” when it comes to strength training [i.e., how many more reps you could complete before reaching failure].

“I’d advise working to two to three reps in reserve, but you can go to four if you’re not confident. But the main thing is you want to see a change in the speed of movement as you fatigue through the set.

“I would focus mostly on compound lifts: barbell hip thrusts, Bulgarian split squats, Nordic hamstring curls, and isometric holds and calf raises to add injury prevention. As time goes on, pair it with more plyometric and ballistic exercises, which might be a squat into a box jump.”

“Winter can be a period where you become unstuck from a psychological point of view. What’s important is to find balance. You want the volume, but don’t want to become stale so that by the time you get to the season, you’ve lost enthusiasm.

“If you really push the envelope early, especially with long, cold rides in January and February, by the time you get through to the season, you’re just sick of it. So, I think there’s a very fine line between doing too much training and not enough.”

The founder and head coach of NVDM Coaching in Austin, Texas, Van Der Merwe leads a team of more than 30 coaches supporting over 700 athletes. A former top-50 world-ranked junior tennis player from South Africa, she raced as a professional triathlete from 2010 to 2023 and has coached since 2009. She also leads Ironman U, Ironman’s official coaching certification program.

“Winter is when we raise the ceiling. We reverse periodize, so short, focused threshold and VO2 work comes before the long volume, because every triathlete races at a percentage of their FTP.

“If an athlete raises FTP from 220 to 235 watts this winter and rides an Ironman at 70% of it, race-day power goes from 154 to about 165 watts. Spring then becomes about extending that fitness.”

“Most athletes book a fit in spring, which leaves little time to adapt before racing. Our order is comfort first, then aerodynamics, then power, because the fastest position is the one you can hold for the whole bike leg and still run well afterward.

“In one study, the lowest torso angle tested cost riders about 16 watts at threshold compared with their own positions. Winter trainer rides are the perfect place to build into a new position gradually.”

“This is one most athletes never think about, and it can quietly derail a whole season. Vitamin D drops through the winter, especially for athletes training indoors at northern latitudes.

“A review of more than 2,000 athletes found over half had inadequate levels. Iron stores matter too, especially for female athletes. We ask athletes to get a baseline panel with vitamin D and ferritin now, so their doctor can address anything before the big training blocks start.”

Head coach at KIS Coaching, Cunnama is a former elite professional triathlete from South Africa who won major long-distance races, including Challenge Roth and Ironman Hamburg, and owns two top-five finishes at the Ironman World Championship in Kona. Following his racing career, he became a presenter with the Global Triathlon Network (GTN), sharing his knowledge and experience with a worldwide triathlon audience.

“Everyone knows they should work on their weaknesses over winter, but that usually translates to a broad goal like, ‘I want to work on my swim,’ which then turns into ‘more swimming, less biking and running.’

“I find it more effective to keep a balance in all three triathlon disciplines, but try to get ahead on the things that you always fell behind on last season. Determine which aspect of your training made you feel most underconfident, and then tweak your off-season training to target that area.

“For example, if you found that using paddles destroyed your arms, do extra paddle work. If hills were your nemesis on the bike, hit the hills (or simulate them on the trainer). Rather than tackling physical limitations, target the mental hurdles – use the off-season to get to a place where you love the sessions you hated last season.”

“It is hard to make changes to technique during the season when you have volume goals in training, because technique changes (or position changes on the bike) require you to only do as much of the new technique as you can sustain, and no more.

“You can’t ingrain a new technique when the second half of your session is falling back to the old technique! So, make those changes in the off-season and slowly build back that technique better. The advantage of triathlon is you have two other sports to keep you fit while you reset your technique in the third sport.”

A highly respected triathlon coach, Tilbury-Davis has worked with professional and age-group athletes since 1995. Through Tilbury-Davis Coaching, he has coached leading athletes such as Lionel Sanders and Ashleigh Gentle. Based in Finland, he works with a small group of international athletes.

“Efficiency of movement sounds vague, but while I’m a big proponent of doing strength and conditioning work throughout the year, winter is a time to understand that swimming, biking, and running all require expression of force from the core – when I say core, I effectively mean from the knees to the chest.

“You’re talking around 64 different muscles and creating the capacity to have a stable base to express force from will improve your body alignment in the water, your ability to maintain an aero position on the bike, and your ability to have hip extension and knee drive in the run. It centers around doing the kind of exercises that are multi-plane, multi-muscle recruiting as part of a several-times-a-week program.

“For example, you see a lot of triathletes train with a Masters group and the swim coach says to do a high elbow or chicken wing drill. The reality is that 99% of triathletes do not have sufficient mobility to swim in a manner that a swim coach would like. So, to step back, I would say to improve your swimming, go away and work on your thoracic and scapular mobility.”

“A lot of people don’t talk about saddle choice. We all buy expensive running shoes that are made out of expensive foam that breaks down over a period of time, but we forget that saddles are also made out of foam.

“If you’re serious about maintaining a good position on the bike, you probably should be changing your saddle once a year and for a pro that might be twice a year because the foam in the saddle breaks down the same way that the foam in a running shoe breaks down.”

“Get used to having to cope with uneven surfaces on the run, shortening and lengthening your stride length, stepping over rocks and roots, dealing with off camber, on camber, dealing with gravel, sand, mud, all of those proprioceptive stimuli that vary significantly improve your body’s ability to be efficient. A worst-case scenario for me would be an athlete that just runs on a treadmill the entire winter at a very narrow bandwidth of running paces.

“A good way of explaining this is that people talk about the way the Kenyans train. They do this famous long run in Iten where it’s a progressively descending pace. But what’s special about that workout is that they’re running on trails, gravel fire roads, wooded areas, and gradient changes. Probably the most powerful thing about that run is that they’re working on different surfaces, different terrains, different obstacles, different gradients, while they’re still working on a physiological stimulus.”

“That’s probably when people ask me what’s the number-one most important session for Ironman training: I would say go run on trails before anything else, because it builds resilience and strength, which is what you need for an Ironman.”

#8835. These 10 Brooks Running Shoes Will Help You Run Your Best Miles Yet

From the Ghost to the Glycerin, Brooks is our go-to brand for comfiest trainers.

Editor’s Note, November 18, 2026: Brooks has a mega sale going on right now. The Glycerin Flex, Adrenaline GTS 25, and Glycerin Max 2 are on discounts as high as 25% off. The Adrenaline GTS 26 is out now—we’ll be getting in feedback soon. All this is to say, better stock up on the 25 before it’s gone.

In 1977, the Vantage was the first Brooks shoe to top our charts. The running renaissance began several years prior, when Frank Shorter won the 1972 Olympic marathon in Munich. Two years later, the shoe industry would be changed forever with the introduction of ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) foam, which was lighter, softer, and had more rebound than the rubbers used in midsoles around that time. Our editors knew Brooks had a winner when we tested the Vantage.

Almost half a century later, the brand is still dazzling us with its innovations and earning prizes in the 2026 Runner’s World Shoe Awards. And to think the company started out more than a hundred years ago manufacturing ballet slippers and bath shoes.

Since the 1970s, Brooks has solely focused on upping the ante in shoe tech. The Vantage also introduced the varus wedge, which was basically a medial post used to help with instability caused by overpronation. Now the varus wedge is dated and has been replaced with Brooks’s “GuideRails” system. EVA is also being phased out with improved foams that are bouncier and even softer.

Gear Up for Training Season: Best Running Shorts ● Best Socks for Runners ● Best Running Watches

Our team vets hundreds of shoes a year and distributes models to more than 250 local testers for evaluation. Shoe testers of different levels, ages, arch heights, and gait patterns log at least a hundred miles before submitting feedback on a shoe’s fit, feel, and ride. Keep returning for more updates as we make our way through 2026’s hottest Brooks releases.

The Glycerin 23 knocked the Ghost 18 out of Best Overall this round. While the Ghost 18 is still on this list as Best Daily Trainer, we found during testing that the Glycerin 23 is more foot shape-friendly. Testers liked the broader platform and toe room, as well as the bouncy and supportive cushioning. The shoe is my go-to for daily training—but the long run is where it shines.

I usually grab a carbon-plate shoe for my long runs, especially when I’m less confident about being out on the road for two hours at the beginning of marathon training. But the Glycerin 23’s midsole upgrade convinced me to save my carbon shoes for race day. DNA Tuned is lighter than DNA Loft, the Glycerin’s previous foam, and delivers a springier ride. My legs feel fresh when I power down hills in the shoes. The energy return doesn’t make my double-digit runs feel like a crawl.

The shoe is also available as the Glycerin GTS 23, the stability counterpart. I find the Glycerin GTS 23 slightly stiffer and firmer than the neutral model, but it’s a good choice for runners who need a little more support on their long runs if they’re prone to late-onset overpronation, or if they prefer denser cushioning underfoot.

The Trail Adapt system—which involves a wide base, flexibility in key areas, and adaptable lugs—makes the Cascadia 20 a favorite shoe pick for runners who need more stability off-road.

A minor drawback: the lack of airflow. Testers found the shoe’s upper comfy but said the it ran hot. Despite the need for more ventilation, they described the Cascadia 20 as a solid trail shoe for most surfaces.

“I would rate the Brooks Cascadia 20 highly because it offers an excellent balance of comfort, stability, and protection across a variety of trail conditions,” said tester Julian Caiazzo. “Compared to other trail shoes I’ve worn, it strikes a nice middle ground between lightweight performance shoes and heavily built hiking-focused models. The shoe felt secure and reliable on uneven terrain, though it prioritizes durability and confidence over outright speed. Overall, it’s a versatile option for runners and hikers who want one shoe that can handle a wide range of trail adventures.”

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com

Brooks has categorized its shoes to help runners choose the best pair that fits their running style and preferred experience. I’ve been a Brooks die-hard since my high school days. For the past 20 years, I’ve been keeping tabs on product updates and saying goodbye to discontinued lineups (taps for the PureProject minimalist list). Here’s a breakdown of everything you need to know—foams, stability tech—about Brooks’s footwear.

One helpful way to choose Brooks shoes is by knowing Brooks’s foams. The kind of foam determines the type of running experience the shoe is meant for.

Through the decades, Brooks revved up its EVA foam, developing MoGo foam in 2006, and then DNA foam in 2013. Known for its adaptive midsole cushioning, DNA has undergone an evolution of its own, breaking into its own subcategories in types of shoes.

Runners looking for a more cushioned shoe will want to try trainers with DNA Loft midsoles. DNA Loft v3, for example, which is featured in the Ghost 18 and the Adrenaline GTS 25, is nitrogen-infused EVA and rubber. It has large cells of air to pack in cushioning without adding extra weight.

At the beginning of 2025, Brooks released the Glycerin Max which showcased DNA Tuned. In developing DNA Tuned, the brand’s team found they could manipulate the cells creating larger cells in the heel and smaller cells in the forefoot. In an interview with Runner’s World, Brooks Chief Product Officer Carson Caprara explained how this dual-cell cushioning softens landings and becomes a springboard for responsive toe-off.

For runners looking for shoes for speedwork or racing, they should look for shoes with DNA Flash or DNA Gold; the latter is a pure PEBA midsole. DNA Hype is a combination of EVA and PEBA. We found in our testing its good for speedwork.

Before the Adrenaline GTS launched in 1999, Brooks had set out to build off of the success of the Addiction. Runners wanted a more flexible version of the stability shoe, and so, the Adrenaline GTS—Go-to-Shoe—was born.

In 2018, Brooks adapted a more holistic approach with stability, implementing a guide rails system into its shoes. The guide rails system has two dense foam pieces in the midsole, one on the medial side and one on the lateral side. These foam pieces reduce your foot from rolling outward and inward when your form becomes erratic due to overpronation or late onset overpronation.

Now redefined as Go-to-Support, GTS Brooks shoes are the stability counterpart of their neutral models. In this way, you can easily find your favorite Brooks trainer with just a little extra support in the midsole and not much else changed with the shoe.

Screen-printed mesh provides lightweight structure with more airflow and flexibility.

This sticky outsole compound aids grip and wet-surface traction on trail shoes.

What’s the best Brooks shoe for beginning runners?

We always recommend the Ghost because it provides plenty of supportive cushioning without being too bulky. It’s an ideal daily trainer for beginners to start with as an offshoot.

How does the Hyperion Elite 6 compare to other carbon shoes?

According to testers, the Hyperion Elite 6 feels less softer and more accommodating compared to other super shoes they’ve tested. The new DNA Gold midsole adds more edge compared to the Hyperion Elite’s DNA Flash foams, with testers saying the rebound is comparable to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4 or Saucony Endorphin Pro 5.

Does Brooks have bargain-priced shoes and how do they stack up to more expensive models?

The Launch 12, included on this list, has a fit and feel almost on par with more expensive models. It’s not as responsive compared to $140 to $160 trainers due to its EVA cushioning, but it delivers a smooth ride.

The ultimate domestic travel rewards benefit for families and couples

Imagine this: you book a flight for yourself, and your spouse — or your best friend, or your mom — flies with you for the cost of taxes alone. Not a discount. Not a sale. Completely. Free. For up to two full calendar years. That's the Southwest Companion Pass, and it is, without question, the single most powerful perk in all of domestic travel rewards. The ChooseFI community has a saying: if you only ever pursue one travel rewards strategy in your life, make it this one. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A round-trip Southwest flight from Denver to Cancún might run $400 per person. A family of four flying during spring break? You're looking at $1,600 cash. But with the Companion Pass, you pay for two tickets and the other two fly nearly free (taxes and fees only) — cutting your out-of-pocket cost in half, every single flight, for nearly two years. Run the numbers over a year of typical family travel and you're looking at **$2,000 to $8,000 in total value** from a single benefit. The CPP (cents per point) range here — **1.5 to 5.9 cents per point** — is what makes this genuinely remarkable. Southwest's Rapid Rewards program values points at roughly 1.4 cents toward any flight. But the Companion Pass doesn't just redeem points efficiently; it *doubles the value of every redemption you make while it's active*. That's the pricing inefficiency the loyalty system has quietly built in, and the FI community is uniquely positioned to exploit it. Think about what 135,000 points normally buys: roughly $1,890 worth of Southwest flights. Solid, but not earth-shattering. Now attach the Companion Pass, and those same points — redeemed strategically over two years — effectively unlock $3,780 or more in flight value for your household. No blackout dates. No seat restrictions. No change fees. Just book, fly, repeat. This isn't a first-class lounge or a lie-flat bed over the Pacific. It's something arguably more valuable for the FI-minded family: **sustainable, repeatable, nearly free domestic travel** that works with your actual life.

The Companion Pass isn't a points redemption — it's a status benefit. That distinction is everything, and it's the insight that separates people who get this from people who miss it entirely.

Here's how it works: Southwest grants the Companion Pass when you earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. Once you hit that threshold, you designate one person as your companion, and that person flies with you on every flight — paid or points — for the remainder of that calendar year plus the entire following calendar year.

The key word is "earn." Points transferred in from partners count. Credit card signup bonuses count. Shopping portal purchases count. Almost every way you accumulate points counts toward the 135,000 threshold — except points purchased directly from Southwest.

The pricing inefficiency here is a calendar arbitrage opportunity. If you earn the Companion Pass on January 2nd, you get it for the rest of that year and all of the next year — nearly two full calendar years of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it on November 15th, you get roughly 13 months. The strategy is to time your credit card signup bonuses to post in January, maximizing your benefit window.

Most ChooseFI members build their 135,000 points through a combination of strategies:

Chase Ultimate Rewards → Southwest Rapid Rewards (1:1, Instant) Chase transfers to Southwest at a 1:1 ratio and the transfer is instant — points appear in your Rapid Rewards account within minutes. This makes Chase points (earned on cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Ink Business cards) the most efficient fuel for this strategy.

Marriott Bonvoy® → Southwest Rapid Rewards (3:1, 1-5 days) Marriott transfers at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Southwest point), and transfers take 1-5 days. This is a less efficient path — use it only if you have a surplus of Marriott points and no better option.

The most reliable path to 135,000 points is stacking Southwest credit card signup bonuses. Southwest's consumer and business cards frequently offer bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points each. A couple who each opens one card, or one person who opens both a personal and business card, can often hit the threshold with signup bonuses alone — before spending a dollar on the portal.

Since Southwest charges no fuel surcharges on award flights and points never expire, there's no penalty for building this balance over several months. The Rapid Rewards program is revenue-based with dynamic pricing, meaning points cover the full fare including taxes — no hidden redemption fees to erode your value.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account and your Southwest Rapid Rewards account and tally your existing points. You need 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points earned in a single calendar year to trigger the Companion Pass. Note: points already sitting in your Rapid Rewards account from prior years don't count — you need to earn 135,000 in the target calendar year.

The optimal window is October through December of the prior year. Apply for Southwest credit cards (personal and/or business) so that your signup bonuses post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Verify with Southwest's current card offers — signup bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points are common. A couple can each apply for a card; a solo pursuer can apply for both a personal and a business card if they have qualifying self-employment income.

Call Chase or Southwest after your first statement closes to confirm when points will post. Timing is everything.

Once your signup bonuses post, calculate how many points you still need. If you're short:

Southwest will notify you by email once you've crossed 135,000 qualifying points. Log into your Rapid Rewards account at southwest.com and navigate to "My Account" → "Companion Pass" to confirm the benefit is active.

You can designate — and change — your companion up to three times per calendar year. Name your most frequent travel partner first. Go to southwest.com, log in, and find the Companion Pass section to add their name and contact information.

Searching is simple: go to southwest.com and search any route. Toggle between "$ Dollars" and "Rapid Rewards Points" to see your cost. When you book with points and your companion is designated, Southwest will automatically prompt you to add your companion to the same flight. Your companion pays taxes only — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights.

Pro tip: Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. For peak travel like spring break or holiday weeks, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens.

The Companion Pass works because Southwest treats it as a status benefit rather than a points redemption. Most airline companion programs require you to burn miles for the second ticket or limit usage to specific fare classes. Southwest flips this model: once you earn the pass, your companion flies on every single flight you take — paid or award — for the remainder of the qualifying year plus the entire following calendar year. The only cost is taxes. Because Southwest has no blackout dates, no fuel surcharges, and no change fees, the pass amplifies in value with every trip you take. The January-earning calendar arbitrage is the key optimization that turns a good benefit into an extraordinary one.

Let's make this real. It's March, and your family of four wants to spend a week in Orlando this July — theme parks, pool time, the works.

A quick search on southwest.com shows round-trip flights from Chicago Midway to Orlando for $320 per person. For four tickets, that's $1,280 cash. Standard family travel math: painful but doable.

You have the Companion Pass active, earned back in January. You book two tickets: yours at 22,000 Rapid Rewards points (worth ~$308 at 1.4 cents per point), and your spouse's ticket at $5.60 in taxes as your designated companion. Your two kids? You use 44,000 more points for their tickets. Total out-of-pocket: 66,000 points + $11.20 in taxes.

Let's value those 66,000 points at their Chase transfer cost — you transferred them 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards, where they were worth roughly $825 in travel via the portal. But by pairing them with the Companion Pass, your spouse flies nearly free, effectively doubling your points' purchasing power on this trip.

Cash price: $1,280. Your cost: 66,000 points + $11.20. That's a CPP of roughly 1.9 cents per point on the base redemption — but accounting for your companion flying nearly free, the effective CPP on the entire trip rockets to 3.8 cents per point. Well within the 1.5–5.9 cent range where this sweet spot lives.

And here's what makes Southwest specifically wonderful for families: no change fees. Book in March, change in June when your kid's baseball tournament schedule shifts, rebook without penalty. No one in the FI community is paying $200-per-person change fees.

The experience itself? Economy class on Southwest, open seating, snacks, and friendly crew. It's not lie-flat business class to Tokyo — but that's not the point. The point is your family of four flies to Florida for a week, and the flights barely register on your annual budget. That's FI-level travel.

Time your credit card applications so signup bonuses post in January of your target year. A bonus that posts January 5th gives you until December 31st of the following year to use the Companion Pass — nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. This single timing decision can mean the difference between 13 months and 23 months of value.

The Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal (rapidrewardsshopping.com) awards points on purchases at hundreds of retailers. Even after you've earned the Companion Pass, continuing to earn Rapid Rewards points means more flights at lower point costs. Treat it like a cashback portal and check it before any online purchase.

Southwest opens availability 330 days in advance. For Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer weekends in popular markets, set a calendar reminder and book the exact morning the window opens. Southwest doesn't have blackout dates, but high-demand flights sell out in Wanna Get Away fare class — the cheapest points tier — quickly.

You can change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. If your life situation changes — a different travel partner, a new relationship, a child aging into a separate ticket — use this flexibility. Just don't burn all three changes frivolously.

Purchased points do not count toward the 135,000 qualifying threshold for the Companion Pass. Don't make this mistake when you're close to the threshold — transfer from Chase instead.

Some people try to earn the Companion Pass in November or December. You'll get it for only a few weeks before the calendar resets. The math simply doesn't work. January earning is the only strategy worth pursuing.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards Performance Business Credit Card (or similar business cards) have separate signup bonuses that stack with personal card bonuses. If you have any self-employment income — freelancing, a side hustle, a rental property — you likely qualify. This is often the fastest path to 135,000 points for a single applicant.

The Southwest Companion Pass was practically invented for the FI-minded family. If you have a consistent travel partner — a spouse, a partner, a parent you visit annually — and you fly domestically more than two or three times a year, this benefit will transform your travel budget.

Minimum points to get started: You need to earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. In practice, this means you either need access to Southwest credit card signup bonuses (which requires good to excellent credit, typically 700+) or a substantial existing balance of Chase Ultimate Rewards points to transfer at 1:1.

How it fits the FI strategy: The Companion Pass is a force multiplier. Every dollar you would have spent on a second ticket stays in your investment accounts instead. Over a two-year Companion Pass window, a couple who takes six domestic trips per year could easily bank $2,000-$4,000 in travel savings — real money that compounds.

Who this is NOT for: Solo travelers get zero benefit from the Companion Pass. International travelers who primarily fly non-Southwest routes won't find much use here. And if you're averse to economy class or require a specific airline's premium cabin, this redemption isn't your path.

The Southwest Companion Pass earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is almost entirely about the *earning*, not the booking. Once you have the Companion Pass, booking is literally the simplest award experience in travel rewards: search southwest.com, find your flight, click "Add Companion." There are no partner airlines to navigate, no availability calendars to decode, no call centers to endure. It's a 5/5 on ease of booking for a reason. The moderate rating comes from **three earning challenges**: **1. The credit requirement.** Southwest credit cards require good to excellent credit. If you're early in your credit-building journey, this strategy may need to wait 12-18 months while you strengthen your profile. **2. The timing discipline.** Earning the pass is straightforward, but earning it in January takes planning. You need to apply for cards 2-3 months in advance and coordinate signup bonus posting dates — something most people have never had to think about. **3. The 135,000-point threshold.** This is a real number. It requires intentional credit card strategy, not casual spending. For a single applicant without a business card, it may require supplementing with Chase transfers or portal activity. **How to overcome these challenges:** - Start planning in **October or November** for a January earn target - Check whether you qualify for a Southwest business card — it dramatically simplifies reaching the threshold - Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal year-round to passively accumulate qualifying points If you've successfully applied for a travel rewards credit card before and you have a consistent travel partner, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has helped hundreds of families earn the Companion Pass — and not one of them regretted the effort.

Open a personal and/or business Southwest credit card so that signup bonuses of 50,000 to 75,000 points each will post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Call to confirm when points will post after your first statement closes.

Once signup bonuses post, calculate your gap. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards at 1:1 (instant) to fill any shortfall. Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal for additional earning on everyday purchases.

After Southwest confirms your Companion Pass, log in to southwest.com and designate your travel partner. Book flights as normal — Southwest will prompt you to add your companion for taxes only ($5.60 each way domestic).

#8832. 5 Pain-Free Arm-Building Alternatives to Barbell Curls

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

The barbell biceps curl is arguably a cornerstone of arm day as well as a favorite among gymgoers.

But even with its popularity in the weightroom, there are subtle issues that could come from barbell curl, the main one being a straight bar could be uncomfortable for your wrists.

Unlike dumbbells, which offer more freedom of movement, the barbell doesn’t. That fixed grip might not vibe with your wrists and forearms as the weight gets heavier. With form issues like wrist hyperextension, questionable grip width, and a little too much body English, your wrists may rebel.

This doesn’t mean you should ditch it at the first sign of wrist discomfort. Sometimes, adjusting your grip, cleaning up your form, or checking your ego at the gym door is all that’s needed to start curling without wrist pain.

But sometimes, the barbell and your wrists will not get along.

Next, I’ll break down four common reasons barbell curls strain your wrists and what you can do about it. Then I’ll cover five biceps-building alternatives that let you pump up without the pain.

Here are four common reasons barbell curls bother your wrists and how to fix them.

Unlike dumbbells, a barbell locks both hands in a fixed position. Depending on your forearm anatomy, mobility, and grip width, this position may cause wrist discomfort. A barbell leaves little wiggle room, and your wrists may tell you all about it.

Quick Fix: Adjust your grip width for more comfort, or switch to a reverse grip.

As the load gets heavier or you become more fatigued, wrist hyperextension may happen. Instead of maintaining a wrist and forearm alignment, the bar pulls the hands backward. That adds extra demands on a body part that’s already working hard.

Quick Fix: Think knuckles in line with your forearms, and do a partial wrist curl to get your hands in that position.

There’s a time and place for body English, but if it causes unnecessary discomfort by pulling your wrist out of neutral during the curl, reconsider your strategy.

Quick Fix: Lighten the load, cut the set short when excessive momentum takes over, or use a three-second eccentric to slow things down.

Your forearms stabilize your wrists, and if you’ve already done a lot of grip work, your wrists may be tired before you begin. When your forearms and wrists fatigue, your grip may weaken, your wrist position may change, and your biceps will be left unsatisfied.

Quick Fix: If your grip gives out, do direct biceps work earlier in your workout with lighter loads, different grip positions, or the alternative exercises below.

If the form fixes didn’t work, it’s time for the alternative. A good alternative trains the biceps hard while addressing what made barbell curls uncomfortable in the first place.

Angled grips, neutral grips, and even overhand grips may feel better depending on your wrist and forearm anatomy. For example, an EZ bar reduces the amount of supination required, while hammer curls keep your palms facing each other.

Dumbbells, ropes, and resistance bands give your hands and wrists more freedom of movement than a barbell.

Look for exercises that keep your wrists neutral, let you control the lifting and lowering phases, and maintain biceps tension. Dumbbells, cables, and bands each feel different but may let you control the weight better without sacrificing gains.

The bottom line: A good barbell curl alternative should solve your wrist problem without creating a new one.

With that covered, here are five exercises that let you keep building bigger biceps without being married to the barbell.

Each exercise addresses one or more of the problems we discussed earlier, so choose wisely. Also, keep a mirror handy.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from the barbell’s fixed position.

The EZ-bar curl is the closest alternative to the barbell curl without locking the wrist in place. Its angled handles allow your forearms to sit in a slightly more neutral position, which many lifters find more comfortable than the barbell.

Form Tip: Choose a hand position that feels comfortable, and keep your wrists neutral.

Solves: Discomfort from the palms-up grip.

If you’ve been hammering the palms-up position, it’s time to switch. Using a palms-down grip shifts the exercise’s emphasis, placing greater demand on the brachioradialis and brachialis while the biceps still get the attention they deserve. The reverse curl provides a different stimulus and gives you another grip option if wrist pain is an issue.

Form Tip: Keep your elbows close to your sides, curl without body English, and lower with control.

Solves: The difficulty of keeping your wrists aligned during barbell curls.

The rope-cable hammer curl combines the wrist-friendly benefits of the dumbbell hammer curl with a touch of cable magic. This variation gives your wrists and hands more wiggle room, letting you adjust your hand spacing throughout the curl. The cable also provides constant resistance throughout the range of motion, enhancing biceps development.

Form Tip: Attach a rope to a low cable pulley and stand tall with your palms facing each other. Curl the rope toward your shoulders, then let your hands separate at lockout.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from a barbell’s fixed grip.

If barbell curls hurt your wrists, the answer may be to lighten the load and switch resistance types. That’s where the looped resistance band curl earns its place. Unlike a barbell, which provides the same external weight throughout the rep, a resistance band’s resistance increases as it stretches.

And don’t mistake bands for beginner-only equipment. Take a challenging set to near muscular failure with good form, and your biceps will thank you.

Form Tip: Grip the sides with your preferred grip, keep your wrists aligned, and curl toward your shoulders. Lower slowly without letting the band snap your hands back.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from limited freedom of movement.

Unlike a barbell, dumbbells let you rotate your forearms as you curl, moving from a neutral grip at the bottom to a palms-up position near lockout. This rotation is more joint-friendly while still engaging the biceps’ two primary functions: elbow flexion and forearm supination.

Form Tip: Start with dumbbells at your sides, palms facing inward. As you curl one dumbbell toward your shoulder, rotate your palm up. Squeeze your biceps at the top, lower under control, and repeat with the opposite arm.

Sets & Reps: 2–4 sets of 12-15 reps per side

Your biceps cannot tell the difference between a barbell, dumbbell, resistance band, or cable machine. They only care about tension. If that tension comes from a barbell and your wrists are annoyed, why keep hammering it when you have options?

If the form fixes above didn’t work, these five alternatives will help you train for gains without the pain.

#8829. Josh Kerr Says You Probably Don’t Need Water for Runs Under 12 Miles. The Internet Had Thoughts.

His comments have divided runners online and highlighted that there's much more at play than how many miles you're logging.

I've worn a hydration vest exactly once, and it was less than pleasant. The two bottles bounced loosely against my chest, with water leaking down my shirt throughout the run. It was not a flattering look. Every step came with its own sloshing soundtrack. I spent so much time adjusting the thing (despite an across-the-chest strap) that I barely enjoyed my run.

So when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from. During a Reddit AMA hosted by BBC Sport, the Scottish middle-distance star, who casually broke the mile world record in July with a 3:42.66 finish, shared his thoughts on the growing popularity of running vests.

"I'd say that if you're running less than 12 miles, you probably don't need to bring water bottles with you," Kerr said, adding that people running in cities can generally stop at a store if they need something to drink.

For context, we're talking about a world-record holder, Olympic medalist, and world champion in the 1500 meters. He knows a thing or two about logging miles. And while 12 miles might look quite different on his watch than mine, I don't think his suggestion was particularly outrageous.

And because everything is contested on the internet, plenty of people disagree.

Runner @natalie.the.capn shared Kerr's comments on Threads and explained that she wears a hydration belt on every outing so she has somewhere to keep her phone, particularly in case of an emergency. "Funny how men rarely think of that," she wrote.

I do understand her concern. I'm a guy, so I'm definitely not going to pretend I have the same safety considerations that women often face while exercising alone. I also bring my phone everywhere, usually carrying it in my hand because iPhones only get bigger and the pockets on most of my running shorts haven't kept up.

She also pointed out that some of her routes take her six miles or more between places where she can get water, which is an entirely different experience from mine.

I live in New York City, where Central Park has plenty of water fountains (that work ... most of the time) and there's usually a deli within walking distance to snag a Gatorade. I can see why Kerr's approach makes sense here, especially for shorter runs. I've also tried handheld bottles and waist straps, and neither has been particularly enjoyable. Between the bouncing, adjusting, and occasional hand cramps, I'd love to carry as little as possible in my hands.

That changes a lot during marathon training, something I've put myself through four times now, when I'm out for considerably longer and need water to wash down those pasty gels. Aside from the hydration aspect, stopping to buy something, pausing my watch, and interrupting my stride halfway through a long run is a vibe killer.

And I'm certainly not arguing against being prepared. I learned the hard way that sunscreen deserved a permanent spot in my prerun routine after years of neglecting it ended with some casual skin cancer surgery.

The Threads debate, naturally, has brought out some pretty different opinions. One commenter, siding with Kerr, wrote, "Yeah im gonna listen to the guy who runs for a living but thanks." Others pointed out that beginners, slower runners, and people training in hot weather could have very different hydration needs.

They're definitely right about that. Twelve miles is a long way for plenty of runners, no matter what their experience level, and access to water, weather, pace, and individual needs all change the equation. Kerr even acknowledged that people have different reasons for carrying gear, something that seems to have gotten a little lost as his comments made their way around social media.

I still think he has a fair point about how much equipment we sometimes convince ourselves we need on a run. That said, if your vest makes your runs more comfortable or gives you peace of mind, by all means wear it. For me, I'll be keeping my phone close and bringing an appropriate amount of water when I need it.

As for my hydration vest, it's been collecting dust ever since that first outing, and I haven't missed it one bit.

#8828. 8 Sugar-Free Electrolyte Powders That Don’t Suck

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Skratch Labs Unsweetened Hydration Sport Drink Mix

When it comes to staying hydrated during a workout or race, many athletes opt for sport drinks, and for good reason – these optimized blends contain calories, carbohydrates, and electrolytes in an easily digestible liquid. But these drinks also contain a lot of sugar, and though that’s exactly what your body needs during a workout, that’s not the case for the hours of your day not occupied by swim-bike-run.

But the effects of those workouts linger, especially during the summer months, during peak training periods, or even when we’re ill. The more we sweat, the more water and electrolytes we lose, and we can feel it in a lot of ways: brain fog, headache, muscle cramps, and fatigue.

Water, along with electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium, is quite easy to replenish through whole-food sources, but to fill the gaps (or to rehydrate quickly), many endurance athletes also turn to sugar-free electrolyte drinks, which deliver all of the rehydration without the added sugar. These beverages provide a tasty alternative to drinking plain water all day, which may lead to increased consumption.

To be clear, sugar-free electrolyte drinks shouldn’t automatically be touted as a “healthier” option than traditional sports drinks. They often contain artificial sweeteners, which some studies suggest can negatively impact gut health and potentially lead to other health issues (for more on this, read sports dietitian Matthew Kadey’s deep dive on sugar-free formulations). Many also list “natural flavors” in their ingredient list, which could be just about anything: LMNT, an electrolyte drink that markets itself as having “no sugar” and “no dodgy ingredients,” has recently come under fire for hiding maltodextrin, a sugar with a high glycemic index, as a “natural flavor.”

But sugar-free electrolytes aren’t going anywhere anytime soon; in fact, many popular sports drink manufacturers, including Gatorade, now offer low- and no-sugar versions of their flagship beverages to avoid penalties in countries with sugar taxes and to meet growing consumer demand for sugar-free options.

Whether you’re looking for an electrolyte complement to your high-carb fueling strategy on race day or a hydration boost at the office after a sweaty lunchtime run, sugar-free electrolyte drinks may have a place in your daily nutrition plan. Triathlete editors shook up eight no-sugar electrolyte blends in search of the best – here are their picks.

You might pucker slightly while drinking this sugar-free electrolyte mix. With no sweeteners and real lemon and lime juice in the ingredients, it’s a delightfully tangy way to get in some electrolytes when you don’t need a hefty dose of carbs during or after exercise.

The salted margarita flavor is certainly reminiscent of its namesake, so sip it on the patio as a little end-of-the-day treat to yourself in the summer, or heat up your water before adding it for a great way to warm up in the winter. While you can get these as individual serving packs for about $1 each, the resealable bag offers a slightly more eco-friendly option that saves you 10 cents per serving.

If you detest the taste of stevia but want a palatable everyday electrolyte that supports super light training or days off, Quince offers an affordable option at 67 cents per serving.

With no sweeteners, this mix mostly delivers a salty flavor with a little fruity flair. The citrus flavor is crisp while the watermelon gives off summer vibes, even if you’re using it to recover from a long day of skiing or ice skating with the fam in the winter. But the raspberry was our favorite as the most balanced flavor in the mix. The multi-pack is great if you plan to drink it frequently and don’t want to get burnt out on any one flavor.

If you like lemon-lime Gatorade, you’ll love this formulation from LMNT. The flavor is oddly reminiscent of the neon-green drink served at the soccer games and track meets of your youth, but without the eyebrow-raising ingredients. (As mentioned above, however, LMNT is currently facing accusations of using maltodextrin as a “natural flavor,” which may negate the halo effect for some customers.)

With 1,000mg of sodium, this is a super-salty blend that takes some getting used to at first; we recommend diluting it in more water or trying only half a packet until your taste buds adjust. But after a long ride in the summer sun, the salt and citrus combo hit the spot much like a margarita at your favorite Mexican joint for post-ride burritos.

Instead of loading up on sodium, Just Ingredients follows a 3:1 ratio of potassium to sodium, along with multiple other electrolytes like calcium, magnesium, and chloride. All of this is derived from real-fruit sources: the first three ingredients listed on the package are guava, peach, and mango. This makes for a pleasant flavor, though the formulation is very clumpy, no matter what method is used to shake or stir the powder into water. Try blending into a smoothie for a cool, tropical treat instead.

Cure’s Hydrating Electrolyte Mixes follow the World Health Organization’s Oral Rehydration Solution formula recommendations for the ideal ratio of water, glucose, sodium and potassium to facilitate rapid rehydration.

Despite the presence of stevia and monk fruit as sweeteners, no chemical taste is present, and the watermelon flavor actually tastes like watermelon, not an artificial dupe of it. For best results, shake vigorously and serve ice-cold (paper umbrella optional).

Led by top triathlon coach Natasha Van Der Merwe, Raw Nutrition’s endurance line has gained a steady following with athletes looking for a comprehensive approach to nutrition and fueling. They’ll find it in this formulation, which contains not only the essential electrolytes but also vitamins C, B6, B12, and taurine.

The mix dissolves well and goes down smooth – best of all, the fruit punch flavor is reminiscent of Hawaiian Punch, making it a nostalgic delight to drink both in and out of workouts.

Made with five real fruits (raspberry, coconut, lemon, lime, banana), a sprinkling of beet powder for nitrates, and a blend of unique ingredients not typically seen in electrolyte powders (bamboo silica, anyone?), DryWater claims to give athletes “complete cellular hydration.” Indeed, many of the ingredients are backed by scientific research. However, some feel a bit of a stretch – the sweetener derived from katamfe fruit extract, for example, provides natural sweetness without spiking blood sugar. However, there is limited evidence of DryWater’s claims that the ingredient “supports balanced energy levels [and] promotes better digestion.”

The flavor is strong and lingers, leaving a film on the tongue and inside the mouth. To avoid this effect, consider using only half a packet or diluting the mix with more water.

As a trusted supplement manufacturer, Thorne is a go-to for many athletes looking for tested and certified products by NSF, or the National Sanitation Foundation, which conducts independent testing to ensure ingredient lists are accurate and free of ingredients banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency. That peace of mind pairs well with Thorne’s blood orange flavor – the mix hits the salty-sweet balance perfectly, with a flavor profile that never gets old. Add to your water bottle at work or while running errands to top off electrolytes throughout the day.
