#8760. Like Jess McClain, I Took Time Off From Running—and Came Back Stronger. These Signs Mean It’s Time to Step Away.

Plus, the benefits you’ll gain from a break.

They say distance makes the heart grow fonder, and that’s true for me with running. But by “distance,” I don’t mean bumping up my mileage or running farther. I mean taking time and space away from my sport during seasons when I feel burned out, lost, or simply exhausted.

Around this time last year, I went from lifting two to three days a week while training for my first marathon to stopping workouts completely and struggling to get off my couch. The second I crossed the finish line, all I wanted to do was let my running shoes collect dust, avoid my local trail, and avoid stepping foot in the gym for a while.

Professional distance runner and New York City Marathon runner-up Jess McClain previously told Runner’s World she felt similarly about six years ago. At that time, she consistently stopped hitting her paces in her workouts and decided to step back from running—a break that lasted about two years.

In my case, I wasn’t as decisive. For months, I resisted the idea that I needed to take a break.

I’d heard that a month is generally how long you need to recover from a marathon, so I told myself that’s when I would jump into winter base training. But every time I tried to get back out there, I got bored and I struggled to recover from my runs. I waited until summer for the urge to work out again, but it never really came back.

For a while, I felt like getting burned out was my fault, that I must have pushed too hard in training. Looking back now—and with help from an expert—I understand that my break was exactly what I needed to get back to my sport in a sustainable way.

My break from running lasted about nine months, and I came back feeling like the runner I had always been before. Plus, I raced one of my fastest half marathons as my comeback.

Below I offer the telltale signs it’s time for a break from running, what a “break” really means, and the benefits you can gain from stepping away from the sport for a while—even if it seems impossible to do so at first.

The farther away I got from my training cycle, the more I realized how much I overtrained. I’d been strength training for 90 minutes three times a week with heavy weights while balancing 30-plus-mile weeks and 20-mile long runs. As I gained more perspective after my race ended, I noticed signs that I was in desperate need of a break.

“Pay attention to trends and patterns [throughout your training],” Erin Ayala, PhD, a sports psychologist, certified mental performance consultant, and founder of Skadi Sport Psychology, tells Runner’s World. “We all have bad days where the numbers aren’t coming together or a run feels harder than it normally does at a given pace. But if it continues to occur, then it can definitely be a sign to take a break,” she says.

Ayala says there are three main factors that often lead to athletic burnout. Here’s what each can look like, and how I experienced them.

You might need to take a step back if you find yourself hitting training plateaus despite putting in your best efforts.

I picked a training plan that included paces far too fast for my fitness level at the time, so every interval workout I did felt difficult, and my paces never really improved. The longer the intervals got, the farther I was from my desired split. But I kept checking off the weekly workouts anyway.

This lack of personal achievement and growth can halt your motivation levels. “When you’re not able to progress and you lose sight of [personal achievements] you’re just going through the motions, that’s a really big red flag,” Ayala says.

After the first month or so, marathon training started to feel more like a chore and I felt really tired and disconnected during my workouts. I figured it was probably normal because I had never run a marathon before, but it turns out that’s not how you should expect to feel daily in your training. “If the workouts are just a grind and you’re having to peel yourself off of the couch in order to get them in, and that’s a sustained pattern, then that’s another big red flag,” Ayala says.

A change in my relationship with running and my “why” meant grappling with my identity as a runner, which Ayala says is the third factor that can contribute to athletic burnout. You might ask yourself questions like, “Why do I even do this anymore?” and “What’s the point?” She says that if those questions linger for more than a week or so, then that’s a sign you might need a break.

By the time I got to the start line, I questioned why I was even there, and all I could do was get through it. “There’s a very real sense of grief and loss, and that’s really scary,” when taking a step back from running, Ayala explains. “Often we hang on quite desperately to our athletic identity when it’s also okay to move on and to do something different.”

Once I knew I needed a break from running, I didn’t quite know how to hit pause.

Then Ayala pointed out that perfectionism can affect your relationship with your sport. And simply hearing that helped me realize why I needed to step away.

There are two types of perfectionists, Ayala explains. The first type is the high achiever, who wants to be the best and perform at the top as much as possible. The second type of perfectionist takes a more “maladaptive form.” These individuals are highly motivated by others’ perceptions and expectations, she says. They might fear failure and generally don’t want to disappoint people.

That second type of perfectionism resonated with me because I realized I was listening to a nagging voice in my head that expected me to give absolutely everything I had to my training. And if I didn’t, I would face that critical voice’s judgment and let it fill me with disappointment and shame.

“Breaks can be helpful because they essentially force you to turn that perfectionistic tendency off. They’re a good way to keep yourself balanced,” Ayala adds.

Once I knew this and decided to take a break, I figured out how to fill my time.

Those first few months after marathon training, I was so excited to not think about running at all. Instead, I looked forward to filling my free time by rebooting my old Webkinz account (an online virtual-pet game popular in the mid-2000s), decorating my new apartment, and watching a lot of TV.

“First, just give yourself time. Then, you can create other bite-sized goals like daily movement, getting outside, spending time with friends, or exploring different hobbies,” Ayala suggests.

When I passed the two-month mark of my break, I took up pottery classes. While that hobby didn’t last, it gave me the space I needed from running.

I knew, deep down, that rest was probably what I needed. But when I took time off, I felt too anxious and ashamed to even enjoy it: I kept thinking about how much time I was wasting and how out-of-shape I felt. “The problem [with athletic burnout] isn’t that you just need to motivate yourself harder. You need to rest in order to get that intrinsic motivation back,” Ayala says.

Ayala explains that if we lose our intrinsic motivation, we often rely on feelings of shame and discipline to keep up with our routine, which ultimately isn’t sustainable.

When I was honest with myself, I found my new “why” for running—my intrinsic motivator—and that was because of how strong, creative, and capable it makes me feel.

One piece of advice from Ayala especially resonates with me: Accept where you’re at and normalize taking a break. “I would argue that getting burned out is a very normal and expected part of being an athlete,” she says. “If you are an athlete long enough, you are going to get burned out at some point and that’s okay. It doesn’t mean that you’re doing something wrong.”

Once I accepted that I was dealing with a longer-term case of burnout and some depression, I began to see light at the end of the tunnel. I set bite-sized goals, per Ayala’s suggestion, and began by committing to running just five minutes a day for a month. With that, running clicked for me again.

Looking back on my time away from running, I don’t view it with shame or anxiety anymore. I see it as both a period of my life when I learned about myself as an athlete and about how my brain works. It was also a time of physiological and mental recovery from so much training stress.

By stepping away, I unlocked a new life experience that can help inform me if—and probably when—I experience burnout again. That perspective shift alone lifts so much weight off my shoulders.

Plus, I’ve come back to the sport now feeling refreshed. I ran one of my fastest half marathons and feel ready to tackle another training plan. I have the drive to set and achieve goals again. And that’s an irreplaceable benefit to taking some time away.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#8759. The Real Grand Theft

Editor-in-chief Chris Foster on why Grand Theft Auto 6 costs more than you think (Photo: Donald Miralle/Getty Images)

Everything has a price, and I think the cost of Grand Theft Auto 6 — the much-anticipated sixth installment of one of the most successful video games in history — is far too high.

And I’m not talking about the cost to your wallet.

Triathletes know all about expensive things: Tri bikes now start around $3,000 and rise (quickly) up from there; running shoes now routinely crack $200; and now we’ve got $270 swim caps. And don’t even get me started on entry fees — the 2026 Hawaii Ironman World Championship, for instance, topped $1,800, granted that’s easily our sport’s crown jewel, but even a new event like 70.3 Utah still rings in around $500.

And even once you factor in the hard out-of-pocket expenses for equipment, entry fees, pool access, coaching, travel, accommodations, and so on, there’s still that looming cost of your time.

If a midpack triathlete did our most popular 70.3 training plan, they’d spend about 150 hours of training over the 20-week plan. For our 16-week Olympic-distance plan, a triathlete would rack up about 65 hours of training. That’s a pretty big chunk of life, but I know I’m preaching to the choir, as all triathletes know that our sport requires a big time commitment.

However, there’s good news: We know that much of that time can be spent outside; we know that — when done correctly — swimming, biking, and running are very healthy endeavors; and we know that much of that time can be spent with others. To that last point, for better or for worse, even just the act of going to a race forces us to participate within a community.

In a digital world that competes ferociously for our attention (think: social media, TV, AI, and so on), giving your precious and valuable attention — your time — to swimming, biking, running, and triathlon will do more for your physical and mental health than getting hooked and strung out on a screen for hours.

So it’s here, in the obsession over the release of GTA 6, that as the leader of an outdoor-related title — and within the context of an era of critically dangerous social disconnection and physical isolation — I find myself confused about why the larger culture is celebrating the creation of something that will drain our attention and time like a dystopian plug in the back of a Matrix battery-person’s skull. I just can’t celebrate.

On one hand, a video game centered on crime and violence is probably more of a sign of the times than a cause for rising crime rates in real life. I’ll succumb to a little bit of Qoheleth-level despair recognizing here that “what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun.”

And of course this is an outdoor sports publication, not Morality Weekly, but I still can’t shake another quote from the bestselling book of all time: “The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness.”

GTA 6’s content notwithstanding, from my position in outdoor/endurance sports, I certainly can’t quite abide when our culture treats the release of a video game like a high holy holiday. Especially when it comes at such a high cost.

Set aside the hard price tag of a gaming console and game (let’s say less than $1k), which is actually relatively low compared to a hobby like triathlon, and keep your eyes fixed on the time cost and quality.

Experts from IGN note that Grand Theft Auto 6 took their editors between 42 and 115 hours to complete the new release. It’s probably a good guess that the average gamer would spend 80ish hours to noodle around in that virtual environment. That’s a lot of “life spend.”

And unlike many other video games, it’s time spent, well…alone.

GTA 6 has no multiplayer mode as of this writing (though it could come). This means there’s no opportunity to connect with other people — even remotely — during gameplay. You can’t commit crimes alongside your buddies in the living room; you can’t fire at police alongside friends in Sweden, Hong Kong, or France. You’re alone, for 60 hours, stealing cars and shooting people. You interact only with that world and the characters coded into it.

Now I won’t be entirely obtuse here — not everyone can physically train for a triathlon; not everyone has time or safe access to a place where they can spend 65-150 hours outdoors, even if they wanted to.

However, there is a large proportion of people whose time spent playing a video game (alone) will prevent them from being outside (with others) — moving their bodies through nature in some way, shape, or form.

That’s why, rather than relish the empty streets and bike paths that have been reported across major metropolitan areas this week, I’ll be hoping that once the game ends and the credits roll (do video games have credits?), folks will head back outside to get a refund for time better spent.

#8758. 13 Best High-Tech Home Gym Products and Fitness Gear

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Home-gym gear has gotten a lot more interesting over the last few years. Smart resistance systems can replace entire cable stations, adjustable dumbbells can cover serious strength work in a small footprint, and recovery tools have become much easier to work into a normal routine. The useful stuff still comes down to one question: does the technology or design actually make training better?

We’re using “high-tech” broadly here because innovation doesn’t always need a screen or app. We personally tested every product on this list alongside plenty of other home-gym and fitness gear, and these stood out for solving real training, space, or usability problems in a meaningful way.

High-tech gear can get feature-heavy fast, so it helps to narrow your decision to what will actually improve your training and fit your space.

Start with what the product actually does once the workout begins. Useful technology should give you something you can feel or use, whether that means better resistance control or feedback that guides the session. A long feature list carries little weight if you don’t use most of it after the first few workouts.

Home-gym equipment has to live in the space long after the novelty wears off. A larger system can earn its space by replacing several other pieces of equipment, while compact gear should be easy to store or used often enough to justify keeping it around. The best designs make the setup easier to train in without creating another piece of equipment you’re constantly moving out of the way.

The Gym Monster 3 can cover enough of a strength program that it feels like the centerpiece of a home gym. During testing, the adjustable cable positions and digital resistance gave us plenty of room for compound work and accessory training without surrounding the unit with weight stacks. One-pound load changes are especially useful when a larger jump would throw off the set’s intent.

Speediance also gives you several ways to control the machine while you train. Smart Spotter monitors movement speed and can reduce resistance when a rep starts to stall, while the Bluetooth ring lets you engage or release the load without reaching for the touchscreen. Programmable cable engagement gives you more control over where resistance kicks in, which is another useful touch when you’re training alone.

Gym Nano packs a surprising amount of training capability into an 18.1-pound unit. During testing, the 16.7-foot cable gave us enough freedom to get into athletic movements beyond traditional cable exercises, while 220 pounds of digital resistance leaves room for heavier strength work. Sled Mode expands the programming options even further when you want to use the resistance for more dynamic training.

Its performance tracking is equally useful. Nano can establish baseline assessments, save individual set data, and build a training history that lets you compare sessions over time. Metrics such as power, movement speed, and rate of force development give athletes and coaches more to work with than a simple resistance readout.

The FAST Series lives up to its name when you need to change weight quickly. Magnetic pop-pins slide along the side rails to make 10-pound jumps, and you can adjust them with the dumbbell outside the cradle, which works especially well for drop sets. Included 2.5-pound microplates give you smaller loading options when a bigger jump doesn’t fit the exercise.

The weight capacity is just as impressive. These dumbbells can reach 125 pounds while measuring only 18.3 inches long at the heaviest setting, giving stronger lifters plenty of room to train without an oversized adjustable dumbbell getting in the way. The 85- and 105-pound versions can also be expanded later, and the cradles grow with them, so you aren’t locked into the weight range you originally buy.

Ab rollouts can be awkward to progress because the jump from a shortened rep to a full rollout can feel pretty big. ZeroWheel gave us much more control over that progression during testing. Motorized assistance can take some load off while you build the movement, then the resistance settings give stronger users somewhere to go once regular rollouts stop being challenging enough. The different motorized modes also open the door to exercises beyond traditional rollouts, giving the device more range than its design initially suggests.

The ZeroWheel Fitness app adds another layer that we ended up appreciating. It includes an exercise library, plus workouts and programs built around the device, so you can pull up a session and get to work without designing your own training. Tutorial videos help with unfamiliar movements, while live performance tracking gives you feedback as you go. That takes some of the planning off your plate and lets you focus on the workout.

The Strive feels different from a typical air bike because resistance isn’t tied entirely to cadence. REP’s Variable Pitch Resistance system changes the angle of the fan blades, so we could make the bike feel heavier without simply pedaling faster. That gave us more control during testing as we moved between longer conditioning work and hard intervals.

REP also addressed some of the smaller annoyances that come with air bikes. A magnetic fan cover lets you control how much air gets blown back at you, and the ratcheting seat adjustment makes position changes quicker than dealing with a traditional pull pin. Those details make the Strive easier to use when you ride it regularly.

The WB7 gives you enough adjustment to get picky about setup. During testing, the backrest and seat positions made it easy to fine-tune pressing angles, and the padding stayed comfortable across flat and incline work. The dual-slot adjustment mechanism also makes changing positions straightforward as you move through a session.

Its weight was one of the biggest practical wins. At 49.8 pounds, the WB7 is much easier to move than many heavy-duty adjustable benches, while its wide base still feels stable under load. Built-in wheels make repositioning it even easier when floor space needs to serve more than one purpose.

The 3-in-1 design gives one box several useful jobs without taking over the room. During testing, we could switch between jump heights just by changing its orientation, then use the same piece for step-ups or other exercises that needed a raised surface. That made it easy to keep in regular rotation without dedicating floor space to several different boxes.

The inner wood core provides a stable platform, and REP uses textured vinyl on the exterior for better grip. The cover is also removable, making it easier to clean or replace after enough training sessions. The smaller sizes are light enough to reposition without much trouble.

The PacerMini fits easily into a home office or small training space. During testing, the low profile and transport wheels made it easy to move when you needed the floor space for something else, and 0.1-mph adjustments gave us enough control to settle into a comfortable walking pace.

The wireless remote makes those adjustments easier when the treadmill is tucked under a desk, since you don’t have to reach down to change speed or stop the belt. The 3.0-mph top speed keeps it firmly in walking territory, while the two incline positions give you another way to change the effort.

Traditional cardio workouts can feel drab and dull. FightCamp hits different—literally—especially for anyone looking for a combat-sports conditioning program at home that brings the feel of a sweaty, old-school boxing gym to the climate-controlled comfort of your living room.

FightCamp has been around since 2018, offering reassurance that it’s an established brand when you’re investing in equipment. Its freestanding heavy bag is a good fit for both boxing and Muay Thai practitioners. The platform offers more than 3,000 on-demand workouts, led by a roster of experienced trainers. You can track every punch and kick in real time and get detailed insights into strike type, speed, and total output.

What’s also reassuring is that FightCamp continues on making improvements. Its recently launched Gen 3 trackers make it easier to monitor your progress—no console required. Up to four compact trackers—two worn in your wraps, with two optional trackers for kickboxing—pair with your phone or tablet to measure each strike in real time.

Technique workouts score punches for accuracy, while FightCamp WORK, launched in June, can now tracks sessions on any bag, anywhere, with mitts, or during shadowboxing. One of its features, Drills, allows you to run either a featured drill, or create your own, set a target for each round, and records and measures your personal bests from week to week.

The cordless setup is what immediately separates the FT-130A from more traditional compression systems. Each boot has its own controller, so there’s no separate pump or hose setup taking over the floor around you. Built-in pressure sensing also helps the system adapt compression around the shape of your legs, which takes some of the guesswork out of dialing in a session.

You still get plenty of manual control when you want it. Eleven pressure levels let you adjust how aggressive the compression feels, and the two boots can sync automatically or operate independently. That independent control also lets you use a single boot when only one leg needs attention.

The Go 3 was easy to keep in regular rotation because it doesn’t feel like another bulky recovery tool to haul around. At 1.6 pounds, it fits comfortably in a gym bag, and USB-C charging means one less proprietary charger to keep track of. Five speeds give you enough room to adjust how aggressive you want the percussion to feel.

Hyperice also includes a carrying case, and the Go 3 is TSA-friendly for carry-on travel, which fits the portable angle well. The flat and wedge attachments covered the basic areas we wanted to hit during testing, while up to four hours of battery life means it can go through several sessions before needing a charge.

The fēnix 9 Pro makes the most sense for someone whose training doesn’t stay in one lane. Strength sessions, conditioning, and outdoor activity can all feed into the same Garmin ecosystem, giving you a broader view of training load and recovery. Training Readiness and Training Status help organize that information, while newer features such as Stamina Zones and Stamina Curve add more context during longer efforts.

Garmin also makes the watch useful once you leave the gym. Multi-band GPS and onboard mapping cover navigation, while the integrated LED flashlight is surprisingly useful for early starts or nights outside. Select versions also add inReach connectivity, giving users another option if satellite communication is part of the plan.

PLAYLIST+ is what makes the TRI 2 PRO especially interesting. The headphones can record audio from a Bluetooth connection directly to their 4GB of onboard memory, letting you bring streaming music with you when your phone or an internet connection isn’t available. That also solves a major problem for swimmers, since Bluetooth won’t transmit underwater. You can load the headphones before you get in and play everything from memory once you start swimming.

The open-ear bone-conduction design also makes the TRI 2 PRO useful well beyond the pool. You can keep your ears open while running, riding, or training outdoors, and the IPX8 construction can handle full submersion down to 12 feet. The H2O Audio PRO app gives you another way to manage songs, folders, software updates, and PLAYLIST+ content from one place.

We personally tested every product in this roundup and compared each one against equipment used across home gyms, training facilities, recovery routines, and everyday fitness. The goal was to find products where the technology or design made a noticeable difference once the gear was actually being used.

We view that testing through a strength-and-conditioning lens, paying particular attention to how equipment fits into real programming. Useful innovation should give you better training options, make equipment easier to use consistently, or solve a problem that shows up in an actual home gym. Those are the products that earned a place here.
